And the majority, by the nature of the case, cannot coordinate: its numbers are exactly what makes it a crowd, and the moment some fraction of it organizes to contest the rulers, that fraction has become – run the definition – a new organized minority, bidding for the same position. The ruling class, Mosca called the standing winner of this asymmetry, and he traced its forms through history: warrior aristocracies, priesthoods, landowners, the wealthy, and – arriving in his own century – the class credentialed to operate the machinery of the modern state. His anatomy of the class has a refinement that matters for everything this shelf has read, because Mosca saw that the visible rulers are the smaller half of the structure. Below the commanding stratum sits a second, much larger one – the officials, officers, managers, and professionals who transmit the top's decisions and run the daily machinery – and Mosca judged this second stratum the true seat of a society's stability: dynasties and cabinets can fall and be replaced in a season, but let the second stratum rot, or defect, or stop believing, and the regime is finished no matter who holds the palace. A reader of this series has met the second stratum repeatedly without the name. It is Whyte's organization men, Jackall's mazed managers, the middle whose conversion the Social Ethic secured – and Mosca's point relocates the significance of all three books at a stroke: the contest that decides a society's character is not the crowd against the rulers, which the asymmetry settles in advance, but the recruitment, training, and loyalty of the stratum in between. Burnham's readers in nineteen forty-three could be trusted to hear the echo; his previous book had given that last cohort a name. But Mosca's subtler instrument is the one this shelf can use, and it explains Dante's pamphlet from a new side. No ruling class, he observed, ever says it rules by organizational advantage. Every one presents its position through what he called a political formula – a doctrine that translates brute position into rightful authority: the will of the gods, the divine right of kings, the mandate of heaven, the consent of the governed. The formula is not a cynical lie; that is the finding's teeth. The rulers believe it, the ruled believe it, and it functions – it stabilizes, legitimates, and recruits – precisely because it is believed. It is the formal meaning, institutionalized; the Social Ethic that episode six found converting Whyte's organization men, the we-do-not-make-mistakes identity that episode four found at the Post Office's System Five, are political formulas in Mosca's exact sense, working at corporate scale. A formula can rot, and when it does the class it clothed is usually near its end. But no class has ever governed naked. The majority is ruled by organization and consoled by doctrine, and the doctrine is sincere on both sides of the transaction.

Chapter Four: The Reasons That Come Second

If Mosca supplied the school's sociology, Vilfredo Pareto supplied its psychology, and it is the piece a clinician will fight hardest, so it deserves the careful version. Pareto was an engineer and a mathematical economist – the Pareto of the distribution and the optimum – who turned, late, to a vast treatise on how people actually behave, and its central finding can be put in one sentence: most human conduct is non-logical, and nearly all of it is rationalized. Non-logical, not illogical – the distinction carries the whole argument. Logical conduct, in Pareto's strict sense, selects means that objectively connect to ends, the way an engineer sizes a beam; it exists, and it is rare, mostly confined to technical work. The rest of conduct flows from stable underlying dispositions – sentiments, drives, cast of mind; he called their observable expressions residues – and then, because humans are the animal that cannot bear to act without reasons, the conduct gets dressed, after the fact, in justifications. Those he called derivations: the theories, principles, and arguments we produce to explain decisions already made in the sentiment. The derivations vary wildly – this century's natural law is that century's divine will is this morning's data-driven strategy – while the residues underneath barely move; and so, Pareto concluded, to study political argument as if the arguments caused the behavior is to study the paint to predict the ship. Before the objection forms, mark what the claim is not. It is not that people are stupid, or that reasoning never occurs; Pareto spent half his life doing mathematical economics and knew logical conduct when he saw it. The claim is about sequence – that in the domains that matter most to people, the conclusion typically arrives first and the reasoning is dispatched to fetch it – and the clinical literature of this listener's own field has spent the decades since accumulating embarrassing support: the confabulation studies, the motivated-reasoning experiments, the reliable discovery that expert judgment and expert justification can be varied independently. A physician who has watched a tumor board talk itself into the plan the chief proposed in the first minute has seen a derivation assembled live, by six well-trained minds, in perfect sincerity. Pareto's instrument does not say the reasons are worthless. It says the reasons are evidence about the speaker, not about the world – read them the way a diagnostician reads a symptom: not for what they assert, but for what is producing them. Burnham takes from this a corollary aimed straight at reformers: programs, ideologies, and manifestos are derivations almost entirely – you learn what a movement will do not from its stated theory but from the sentiments of the men it selects and the position they are fighting from. And Pareto's second export gives the school its dynamics. Elites, he found, are never permanent; history is a graveyard of aristocracies, and the mechanism of their death is the slow change in the mixture of types at the top – his shorthand, borrowed from Machiavelli, was foxes and lions: the men of combination, maneuver, and deal, versus the men of force, loyalty, and faith. Regimes of foxes rot toward cleverness without nerve; regimes of lions toward rigidity without adaptation; and the circulation of elites – the displacement of one governing mixture by another, sometimes by co-option, sometimes by catastrophe – is, on this account, what political history is made of, underneath whatever the derivations were saying while it happened. History, in the four words of his that outlived the four volumes, is a graveyard of aristocracies – and the sentence's tense is the argument: not battlefield, graveyard; the outcome is never in doubt, only the schedule. A ruling class dies, in his account, mostly by its own filters. It stops admitting the able and ambitious from below – the very types whose energy built it – and the excluded talent does not evaporate; it accumulates outside the walls, unemployed and increasingly organized, until the class within, grown clever and bloodless, meets the counter-elite it manufactured by refusing it. Circulation blocked is revolution scheduled.

Chapter Five: The Story That Moves the Crowd

The school's strangest member supplies its strangest instrument, and Burnham needs him for the piece Mosca and Pareto leave unexplained: if the majority can never rule, what are the majority's great movements? Georges Sorel – French, an engineer for twenty-five years before he began to write – studied the revolutionary syndicalism of his day and located its engine not in its economic program, which he thought mostly fantasy, but in what he called its myth: the general strike, the image of one apocalyptic day when all labor stops and the old world falls. The myth, Sorel insisted, is not a prediction and cannot be refuted by pointing out that the day never comes – that is like refuting a battle flag. It is a body of images that organizes the sentiments of a mass of men, binds them into a fighting unit, and makes coordinated heroism possible for people who will never attend a strategy meeting. Sorel drew the distinction that keeps the instrument honest: a myth is not a utopia. A utopia is an intellectual product – a designed future, detailed and comparable and therefore criticizable, the work of theorists addressed to other theorists. A myth is none of these things; it is closer to a battle hymn than a blueprint, and arguing with it is a category error the myth's carriers experience not as refutation but as confirmation that the arguer is an enemy. The distinction predicts something observable: utopias generate committees and amendments; myths generate discipline and sacrifice; and a movement can be located on the map by which of the two its rank and file would die for. Movements run on myths the way engines run on fuel, and the analytical payoff arrives when Sorel's instrument is bolted to Mosca's: a myth is how an aspiring counter-elite solves the crowd's coordination problem – the political formula of a ruling class that does not rule yet. Burnham, writing in nineteen forty-three, had before him the century's demonstration cases, and his readers did not need them named. What matters for this series is what the assembled machine now claims. Political speech is instrumental, top to bottom: the rulers hold a formula, the challengers hold a myth, the individual holds derivations, and at no level – this is the school's full bid – is the talk what it formally claims to be. Which sets the trap this episode has been walking toward, and part two exists to spring. If every doctrine is a formula, a myth, or a derivation, then what of the doctrine called democracy – and what, precisely, is Burnham's own book? The school's answer to the first question sounds, at first hearing, like the end of all political hope: government by the people has never existed and can never exist; the sovereign majority is the political formula of the modern West, sincere, functional, and false. Yet the book's subtitle is Defenders of Freedom, and Burnham meant it – the claim of part two is that this bleakest of schools, and only this school, explains how real liberty is actually produced and kept. Whether he proves it, what Orwell said about the man making the argument, what became of these ideas in our own century's stranger corners, and the verdict with the dose – next time, The Machiavellians, part two. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Parkinson's Law: The Growth That Needs No Work
item.description: C. Northcote Parkinson's deadpan discovery that administration grows by its own laws – the Admiralty numbers, the two engines of multiplication, the bicycle shed, and why everyone laughed and no one acted.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Navy That Grew by Shrinking

Between nineteen fourteen and nineteen twenty-eight, the Royal Navy conducted an experiment it did not know it was running. Over those fourteen years the number of capital ships in commission fell by about two-thirds – the Grand Fleet that had faced Germany at Jutland was scrapped, treaty-limited, and laid up – and the number of officers and men shrank accordingly. The empire's naval work, by any measure a navy's work can be given, had contracted on a heroic scale. The number of Admiralty officials administering that work rose by seventy-eight percent. Dwell on the shape of that for a moment, because the shape is the discovery. It is not that the administration grew faster than the fleet, which would be ordinary sloppiness. It is that the administration's growth had no visible relationship to the fleet at all – the curve went up, smooth and confident, straight through the largest demobilization in British history, as if the ships were a rumor from another department. A magnificent navy on land, the man who found these figures called it. And he checked the pattern against the opposite case, an organization whose workload was not merely shrinking but heading toward abolition: the Colonial Office, custodian of an empire in liquidation. As the colonies went – India gone, territory after territory following – the Colonial Office grew from three hundred and seventy-two officials to one thousand six hundred and sixty-one in under twenty years, a compounding increase of five or six percent a year, indifferent to the direction of history it existed to administer. Two curves, two departments, one conclusion, and the man who drew it published it in The Economist in November of nineteen fifty-five, unsigned, in that magazine's tradition, in the driest scientific prose he could counterfeit: the growth of administration obeys laws of its own. It has a rate. The rate can be measured. And the work – this is the finding under the finding – has nothing to do with it. The officials would have multiplied at their stately five to six percent whether the fleet had doubled, halved, or sailed into myth. This series has spent eight episodes inside organizations that decide, deceive, and refuse to know things. Tonight's book is about something more elementary, the way metabolism is more elementary than thought. Before the machine can shred a squirrel or script a helpline, it must do the one thing every machine in this series has done without exception. It must grow.

Chapter Two: The Historian Who Kept a Straight Face

The author of the finding was Cyril Northcote Parkinson, and his position, like Whyte's, was the argument's warrant. He was not a disappointed clerk or a crusading journalist; he was a naval historian of entirely respectable output – decades of scholarship on trade routes, dockyards, and the eighteenth-century sea war – holding a chair at the University of Malaya in Singapore, a man who had spent a career in archives where the Admiralty's paperwork accumulates. The essay that made him famous is a parody of exactly the kind of paper his profession wrote: a law stated in the passive voice, factors labeled with letters, a formula with coefficients, the whole apparatus of quantitative social science wrapped around the observation that officials multiply because they are officials. Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion – the opening sentence, now so proverbial that people assume it is folk wisdom, was constructed to sound like a finding from a laboratory. The joke did what jokes do: it got the essay read, then the book of nineteen fifty-seven bought, in the hundreds of thousands, by the very administrators it dissected, who displayed it on their shelves the way a cardiologist might display a jar of cholesterol. And the joke had a cost, which is the reason this episode exists and the reason the sign-off last time said what it said. Stated as comedy, the law was received as comedy. The reviewers chuckled; the ministries expanded. It is the neatest available demonstration of a mechanism this series met in the Davies episodes – an organization's genius for absorbing criticism without transmitting it anywhere that matters – except that here the absorption was cultural, and total, and the anesthetic was laughter. So the useful reading, seventy years on, is to take Parkinson at his deadpan word. Suppose it is not a joke. Suppose it is what it pretends to be: a natural law, with mechanisms. What are they?

Chapter Three: The Two Engines

Parkinson gives two, and each one runs on individually blameless decisions – which by now the listener will recognize as this series' watermark of a real mechanism. The first he states as an axiom: an official wants to multiply subordinates, not rivals. Take a civil servant – he names him A – who finds himself overworked, or believes he does, which the first law guarantees he will, since his work has expanded to fill and then overflow his day. Three exits exist. He can resign, which forfeits pension and standing. He can ask to share the job with an equal – a B hired beside him – which is unthinkable, because B becomes the obvious comparison and the obvious successor. Or he can ask for two juniors, C and D, and this door is the only one that opens sweetly, because two juniors make A a manager: his responsibilities now, by definition, exceed what one man can hold, since three men hold them. Two, note, never one – a single junior would be a B in embryo, a co-holder of the file. There must be enough of them that each controls a fragment too small to threaten anyone. And the arithmetic never rests, because in due course C finds himself overworked – sincerely; the first law is working on him too – and the only door open to C is the door that opened for A. Seven officials, Parkinson calculates with a straight face, now do what one did, and here is the turn where the essay stops being a joke about laziness and becomes a theorem about structure: all seven are genuinely busy. That is the second engine – officials make work for one another. The seven do not divide A's old work and idle in parallel; the fragments must now be coordinated, and coordination is itself work of a special, self-replenishing kind. A draft that one man would have written and sent now circulates for concurrence: C drafts, D disputes the draft on behalf of his fragment, their juniors annotate, A reconciles – and the reconciliation is real effort, applied conscientiously, often late into the evening. The file is genuinely thick. Every hour logged against it was honestly worked. The output – one letter, roughly the letter A would have written alone fourteen months earlier – bears no relation to the input, and no one anywhere in the chain has shirked. Hold this against the shelf and the fit is disquieting. Whyte's pipeline was delivering, in exactly these years, cohorts of well-rounded men selected for their fitness to be C and D – team players, coordinators, men whose skills only exist in groups of seven. And Rao's cynical taxonomy waits at the far end: an organization whose middle grows by fragmenting responsibility into unthreatening pieces is manufacturing its Clueless layer by statute, seven sincere believers per original job, each with a title, none with the file. And the book carries a third mechanism, less quoted than the engines because it is not funny, and Parkinson knew it was not funny: he gave it a deliberately ugly clinical name, injelititis, the disease of induced inferiority. It begins when an organization admits to its senior ranks one man who combines, in Parkinson's formula, incompetence with jealousy – a chief who cannot do the work and knows it, and whose response to ability nearby is not recruitment but removal. Such a man staffs downward: he hires people safely duller than himself, who in turn hire duller still, until mediocrity is not an accident of the org chart but its organizing principle, three ranks deep and self-sealing, because by the third generation there is no one left with the standing to notice what has happened. The infected institution does not collapse; that is the diagnosis's bite. It persists, smug and busy, its officials multiplying on schedule, taking a quiet pride in how little it attempts – and Parkinson's proposed treatments escalate through the essay from transfusion to surgery until he arrives, with the courtesy still perfectly intact, at the recommendation that the terminal case be condemned like a building and its personnel scattered where they cannot reinfect one another. Jackall's readers, eight episodes back, met the mature form of the disease wearing better suits: a hierarchy in which the criterion for rising had detached from the work entirely, and attached to the comfort of the man above.

Chapter Four: The Bicycle Shed

The book's other law has escaped even further into the language than the first, and its vehicle is a committee meeting that Parkinson invents and admits to inventing – a constructed example, flagged as constructed, which this series can therefore retell with a clear conscience. A finance committee faces three agenda items. Item one: a contract for an atomic reactor, ten million pounds. Item two: a bicycle shed for the clerical staff, three hundred and fifty pounds. Item three: the refreshments budget for the committee's own meetings, twenty-one pounds a year. The reactor is approved in two and a half minutes. Most of the members do not know what a reactor costs, or contains, or risks; the two who might understand it cannot explain their unease without a lecture nobody has the vocabulary to follow; and hesitation, at this altitude of money, reads as weakness. The bicycle shed gets forty-five minutes. Everyone has seen a shed. Everyone can hold three hundred and fifty pounds in the mind, has an opinion about aluminum roofing versus galvanized iron, and can propose a saving with genuine, checkable competence. The coffee budget – twenty-one pounds – runs an hour and a quarter and ends unresolved, referred back for further information. Parkinson states the law with his customary lethal courtesy: the time spent on any item will be in inverse proportion to the sum involved. Now put the shelf's instruments on it, because the joke is a diagram of a concept this feed built three episodes ago. The Davies series introduced Ashby's law – a controller can only control what it has the variety to match – and the committee is Ashby's law wearing minutes and a quorum. The reactor's variety exceeds the room's: the members cannot generate distinct responses to its distinctions, so the item passes through them, uncontrolled, transparent as glass. The shed matches the room's variety exactly, and so receives the full governing capacity of eleven adults. Attention is flowing, as it must, along the gradient of what the committee can process rather than what matters – and the sum of those two behaviors, viewed from outside, is an institution that rubber-stamps its catastrophes and litigates its coffee. Parkinson wrote it as farce eighteen years before anyone in this series' bibliography could name the mechanism. That a working diagnostic of variety-mismatch spent those decades filed under humor is itself a datum – the finding was received at the exact altitude of the bicycle shed, priced in the room's currency as an amusement, because that was the variety the culture had available for it. And the committee chapter has a sequel about the committee itself, built from Parkinson's own trade, English constitutional history. Governing councils, he observed, have a life cycle as regular as an organism's. A cabinet begins small – five members, perhaps – and grows, because membership is an honor that costs the chairman less to grant than to refuse; and somewhere past twenty members, on his mock-solemn calculation of a coefficient of inefficiency, stated of course to the decimal, the body crosses a threshold and quietly dies as a decision-making organ. It does not disband. It becomes ceremonial, and the real deciding migrates to a small inner group that meets beforehand over the agenda – whereupon the inner group begins, in its turn, to grow. He traced the cycle through five successive English councils of state: each born small and potent around the sovereign, each swollen with honor into an audience, each survived by a compact successor, from the Curia Regis down to the cabinet of his own day, which was by then comfortably past the fatal number. The whole apparatus of formal governance, on this reading, is a shed of nested sheds – each ring of the org chart a former decision body, preserved in amber at the size at which it stopped working.

Chapter Five: The Case Against, and the Curves That Kept Rising

Now the steelman has run long enough, and the case against deserves its innings, because it is real. Count one: the numbers are curated. Parkinson's Admiralty and Colonial Office series are true, but they are two series, chosen for effect, with no controls – a historian's anecdotes in a lab coat, and he knew it; the lab coat was the joke. An honest account adds that later, sober attempts to test the law have kept finding its footprints: administrative headcount growing independent of enrollment in school systems, of caseload in agencies, of fleet in navies – and, in one study by a team of complexity physicists half a century on, a companion finding across nearly two hundred governments that the larger a country's cabinet, the worse its standard indicators of governance ran, which is Parkinson's committee chapter restated with error bars. The law is under-evidenced by its author and over-confirmed by his critics; the direction of seventy years of checking has been toward it, not away. Count two is heavier: the law explains growth without explaining anything else, and a growth law with no theory of function slides toward a politics. Parkinson's numbers cannot distinguish the seventh redundant official from the safety inspector hired after the fire; a reader who takes the law as identity – and its cheerful cynicism invites exactly the identity dose this series keeps flagging – graduates to the view that administration as such is parasitic, and that view has spent decades as the all-purpose solvent of every audit function some machine found inconvenient. Recall what the Davies episodes established about what organizations do with their perceiving organs, and be careful which knife you hand them. And count three is the one Parkinson's own biography files: nothing followed. The book sold like almost nothing else in its decade, its author became a global brand, lectured to the very ministries he had measured – and the curves did not so much as flinch. Comedy, it turns out, is an accountability sink of its own: the laughter acknowledges the finding, discharges the discomfort, and routes the implication nowhere. The ministries bought the book by the crate, and the purchase was the response – filed, as it were, under refreshments.

Chapter Six: Verdict, Dose, and the Question for Monday

The verdict is easy to state and strange to hold: this is the most accurate book this series has covered per page and the least consequential per reader, and the two facts share a cause. Read it – it is short, it is genuinely funny, and its two engines and one committee will name things you have watched happen this quarter. But read it the way part two of this series learned to read Burnham, with the reception as part of the text: what happened to Parkinson's Law is a case study in the phenomenon Parkinson's Law describes, an organization-culture metabolizing its own diagnosis into merchandise. The dose, accordingly, is one read, taken seriously – which concretely means refusing the book's own tone while keeping its content, the exact inverse of what its first ten million readers did. The prescription pairs it backward with Davies, because the two books are one argument at two magnifications: Parkinson found the metabolism, Davies found the cognition, and an organization that grows without reference to its work will in due course decide without reference to its world. And the question for Monday is the cheapest experiment this series has yet proposed. Take the last meeting you sat through and price its agenda: note what the big item cost, what the small item cost, and where the minutes actually went. If the gradient ran toward the shed – and it ran toward the shed – you have measured your institution's variety the way Parkinson measured the Admiralty, from its own paperwork, and the question that follows is his real bequest: what in this organization is currently passing through us in two and a half minutes, transparent as glass, because none of us can afford to admit we cannot see it? Next time the shelf goes back a step to the book Burnham wrote after the Managerial Revolution, the one episode seven called, quietly, his best – four dead Italians and Frenchmen and a renegade German, assembled into the claim that all government, every government, is the rule of an organized minority, and that freedom survives only where minorities fight. The Machiavellians, part one. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Organization Man, Part Three: The Wife, the Curriculum, and the Exit
item.description: A third part on Whyte, for the material the first two compressed: the corporation's claim on the marriage, the retooling of the American college, what Friedan found at the same addresses, and how Whyte himself got out.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Second Interview

The candidate has done well. The tests came back mid-scale in every dimension, which is where the scoring key wants them; the interviews confirmed a sound, sociable, unspectacular man; the offer is being prepared. One evaluation remains, and the candidate will not attend it. Sometime in the next few weeks, at a dinner, or a company picnic, or a visit to the couple's home arranged with plausible casualness, the organization will meet his wife. It will want to know certain things. Whether she drinks, and how much, and how gracefully. Whether she talks too well or too little, whether she outshines him, whether she resents the moves that are coming – because the moves are coming, every two or three years, and a wife who digs in her heels in Dayton is a logistics problem wearing a dress. Above all it will want to know whether she understands the arrangement: that she is joining too. None of this was hidden, and none of it was fringe. When Fortune surveyed corporate hiring practices at mid-century, roughly half the companies in its study screened wives in some form – formally, with interviews, or informally, over the rim of a cocktail glass – and executives explained the practice to the magazine's reporters without embarrassment, in the reasonable tones of men describing due diligence. The reporter they most often explained it to was William Whyte. Two episodes ago I said that The Organization Man begins with a young man and a personality test. That is true of the book. It is not true of the project, because before the book, before Park Forest, before the appendix that teaches cheating, Whyte's beat at Fortune was the wives. In October and November of nineteen fifty-one he published the articles that made his name inside the trade: a close study of the executive marriage as the corporation's newest acquisition. The book that came five years later moved the wives to the scenery, and part one of this series dinged it for that. But the scenery had been center stage first, and what Whyte found there is the most complete picture anyone drew of the Social Ethic's reach – because the organization's claim on the man could at least be called a purchase. He drew a salary. The claim on the wife was something else, and this episode is about how far that something else extended, at both ends of a career: into the marriage on one side, and backward into the schools on the other, where the organization man was being manufactured before any company had met him.

Chapter Two: The Unsalaried Employee

Stay with the wives, because the nineteen fifty-one material deserves the dwell time the book denied it. What Whyte documented was not a company demanding subservience; it was subtler and more total. The corporation of mid-century had worked out, without any office holding the file, a job description for a woman it did not pay. She managed the household singlehanded so that the man's evenings belonged to work; she moved on command, absorbing each transfer's damage – the abandoned friendships, the schools changed mid-year – and presenting a settled home within weeks; she entertained at the level of the husband's grade, one notch of hospitality per rung; and she performed, at every company occasion, a calibrated warmth: friendly to all, intimate with none, ambitious for him in a way that must never look like ambition of her own. The wives Whyte interviewed knew the rules and could recite them, and the recitation had a shape he had the wit to write down: nearly every rule was negative. Don't outdress the boss's wife. Don't complain about the hours. Don't be controversial, don't be brilliant at dinner, don't drink one past the second. The job was defined entirely by the errors it was possible to commit – which is, if you think about it in this series' terms, the purest expression of the Social Ethic anywhere in Whyte's work. The organization man at least had a ladder; positive performance existed for him, and could be rewarded. For the wife there was no ladder, only a tightrope: nothing to win, everything to forfeit, on his behalf. And the corporations were not sheepish about the arrangement; the ones Whyte studied were proud of it. They ran orientation programs for new wives. They sent them company magazines. Executives spoke warmly, in the interviews, of the wife as a member of the team – the merger, Whyte called it, of corporation and marriage, and what stops a reader in the transcripts is how much of the merging the wives had internalized as their own idea. The ones who chafed mostly blamed themselves for chafing. A belief system that makes the group's pressure feel like personal morality – part one spent a chapter on that definition. Here it is with the office door closed, at eleven in the morning, alone in a court in Park Forest with the coffee circuit due at noon. The book's four hundred pages never quite look straight at her. The magazine series had, five years earlier, and then the project moved on to the man, and the wire between those two facts carries a current this episode will come back to.

Chapter Three: The Pipeline

Now run the claim backward, to before the hiring, because the book's least-quoted section is the one Whyte himself placed first. Part Two of The Organization Man is titled the training of the organization man, and its argument is that the corporation did not need to convert its recruits, because the schools were delivering them pre-converted. The evidence starts with a curriculum audit. American higher education, Whyte found, had been quietly retooled in a single generation: enrollment in the fundamental disciplines – the sciences, the humanities, the things a person studies to know them – was shrinking as a share of the whole, while the practical and vocational tracks swelled, with business administration out front, a degree in the running of organizations as such, agnostic about what the organization does. The chapter titles do the editorializing his prose declines to: A Generation of Bureaucrats. The Practical Curriculum. The Pipe Line. The pipeline was literal. Corporate recruiters toured the campuses each spring like buyers at a livestock show, and Whyte interviewed both ends of the transaction. The recruiters were candid: they were not, on the whole, hunting brilliance. Brilliance specializes, argues, quits; the recruiting profile favored the well-rounded man – his quotation marks again – the B student with activities, the campus committee veteran, sociable, presentable, moderate in all things including curiosity. And the seniors had priced the signal perfectly. The class of the mid-fifties, surveyed about its hopes, wanted the big company, the staff position, the training program; the personnel department's preferences had propagated backward through the pipeline until they had become the students' own preferences, self-applied at nineteen. No coercion anywhere in the circuit – only the Social Ethic completing itself, teaching each stage to want what the next stage selects for. It is the shape this series has since learned to call a feedback loop with the correction removed: the signal that should have run from the work back to the training – what kind of mind does the work actually need? – had been replaced by a signal running from the personnel office to the sophomore, and nothing anywhere in the loop was measuring what the substitution cost, because every station in it was hitting its numbers. Whyte pushed the logic one domain further, into the one this listener works in, and his extrapolation has aged unnervingly well. If the well-rounded ideal reached science, he argued, it would arrive as the team: suspicion of the lone investigator, worship of the coordinated project, funding flowing to the well-adjusted collaborator over the prickly obsessive – the bureaucratization of discovery itself. He wrote that as a warning about General Electric's laboratories. A modern reader who has served on a study section, or watched a grant scored for its team science and its integration plan, can decide for herself how hypothetical it stayed. The pipeline and the wife programs are one system seen at its two ends: the organization reaching backward into the classroom to shape what it would hire, and sideways into the kitchen to enlist what it would not pay. The man in the middle, the nominal subject of the book, starts to look like the system's most pampered component. Both of the claims flanking him were larger than the claim on him – and only his had a union of any kind, even the private union of the cheating appendix. Which raises the question the fifties could not ask, and someone else answered.

Chapter Four: The Problem at the Same Address

Seven years after The Organization Man, a freelance journalist published a book built from surveys of her Smith College classmates and interviews with women in exactly the suburbs Whyte had mapped. Betty Friedan called the condition she found the problem that has no name: the highly educated wife, installed in the successful household, performing the role competently and suffocating inside it, unable even to specify a grievance because the culture had defined her situation as the reward. The Feminine Mystique detonated in nineteen sixty-three, and it is customary to treat it as the beginning of something, which it was. But set it on the shelf next to Whyte and it is also an ending – the closing of a case file he had opened and left on the table. Read in sequence, the two books are a single study in two voices: Whyte establishes the machinery – the screening, the transfers, the negative rules, the court geometry that assigned the coffee circuit its route – and Friedan takes the deposition of the people the machinery ran on. The overlap runs to the details. Friedan's suburban informants describe the same compulsory sociability Whyte diagrammed from the driveways; his organization wife, appraised over the cocktail glass, is her subject a decade into the sentence. Even the two books' blind spots interlock: Whyte saw the system with perfect clarity and registered its cost to the woman as atmosphere; Friedan rendered the cost unforgettable and had less to say about the corporate machinery that billed it. Neither cites the other much, and it does not matter; the American mid-century wrote the two halves of one diagnosis through two writers who happened to be standing on opposite sides of the picture window. For this series the pairing settles a question part one raised and left hanging. The case against Whyte included the charge that the organization man's world rested on an unexamined support, and the fair reply, now visible, is that the fault was not blindness but sequence: Whyte gathered the evidence first, at Fortune, and then wrote the book about the husband. History assigned the book about the wife to someone with standing to write it. What neither book could see from nineteen sixty-three is the epilogue this feed's own century supplies. The corporation eventually stopped screening wives – the practice died of legal exposure and of the two-career marriage – and the claim did not dissolve; it migrated. The modern organization asks the employee directly for what it once asked the household to subsidize: the always-reachable evening, the relocation absorbed without a buffer, the emotional performance at the all-hands. The unsalaried employee was not emancipated so much as merged into the salaried one. Whether that is progress is a fair fight; that it is the same claim, renamed, is just reading.

Chapter Five: The Man Who Took His Own Advice

One thread remains, and it is the one this supplementary episode exists to tie off, because it changes the color of everything behind it. The Organization Man ends, part one of this series said, with an appendix teaching the reader to defend the border of the self – advice for one man at a time, and the case against called it a concession. What the case against left out is what the author did next, which was to take the advice, at scale, in public. In the late nineteen fifties, at the peak of the book's fame, Whyte did the thing his own subjects could not imagine: he left. Not for a rival organization – out. Before going, he used Fortune's pages for one last act of editorial matchmaking, commissioning a piece on American downtowns from an unknown writer at an architectural magazine named Jane Jacobs; the article grew into The Death and Life of Great American Cities, and Whyte's fingerprints are on the founding document of a whole tradition of seeing cities from the sidewalk. Then he spent the rest of his life on the sidewalk himself. Beginning in nineteen sixty-nine, under the wing of New York's planning commission, he set up the Street Life Project, and it was Park Forest's method aimed at public space: time-lapse cameras on plazas, counts of who sat where and for how long, patient maps of how strangers actually use a corner – the same uncanny attention to the geometry of social life, now deployed for the pedestrian against the planner. The findings have the signature Whyte flatness, observation after observation that sounds obvious the moment after it could have ruined a fortune in granite. The best predictor of whether a plaza gets used is the amount of space a human being can sit on – not sculpture, not fountains, not the architect's award. People given a choice of seats want choices: sun and shade, front and back, together and alone, which is why the humble movable chair, price of a bad lunch, outperforms every fixed bench ever value-engineered into a corporate forecourt. Conversations do not migrate to the quiet edges of the sidewalk; they happen in the middle of the stream, people planting themselves squarely in the flow they claim to be avoiding. And over all of it, the finding he let himself state as a law, in a sentence whose hedge is doing comic duty: what attracts people most, it would appear, is other people. The city took him at his word. His counts rewrote New York's plaza zoning – sittable space per linear foot, entrances near street level, so that the privately owned plaza a developer traded for extra floors had to actually function as a public place – and his methods ran the renovation that turned Bryant Park from a mugging ground into a lawn so heavily used it needs a reservation system. It is the same discovery as nineteen fifty-three's, promoted from diagnosis to code: the court geometry that had silently assigned friendships in Park Forest could be flipped, written into law, and made to assign strangers a bench in the sun. The through-line is so clean it reads as designed. The man who showed how site plans assigned friendships in a company suburb spent his last three decades showing how site plans could invite or forbid public life in a city, and the late work carries the early work's moral inverted into the affirmative: architecture is never neutral, so build it for the humans. He died in nineteen ninety-nine, having been, in sequence, the organization's most attentive internal observer and the century's happiest escapee from it. The escape is the verdict this part adds to the series'. Part two closed the account on the twins; this closes the account on the author, and it answers the charge that his prescription conceded too much. Defend the border, keep the self – as advice to a trainee it is thin, and the critique stands. As a description of a life it turns out to be a complete program, because the self Whyte kept had a use: it was the instrument that did the seeing. Every observation this series has spent three episodes admiring was made by a man who filled out the organization's forms, moderately, for twenty years, and never once handed over the observer behind them. The appendix was not a joke and not a concession. It was the author's methods section. And the question to carry into Monday comes from holding his example against your own week: somewhere in your organization there is a border the process is currently probing – a fit being assessed, an enthusiasm being required, a household being quietly billed. Whyte's full teaching is not merely to defend the line. It is that the ground you hold behind it must be good for something; the kept self justifies the keeping by what it goes on to notice. Next time, the queue resumes with a man who watched organizations grow from inside the British civil service and stated what he saw as natural law, deadpan, which is why everyone laughed and no one acted: C. Northcote Parkinson's Parkinson's Law. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Organization Man, Part Two: The Managerial Revolution
item.description: Part two of three: James Burnham's wartime claim that managers were becoming the world's ruling class, Orwell's demolition of it, and the verdict on the pair of diagnoses the whole shelf descends from.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Prophet of the Losing Side

In the spring of nineteen forty-one, with France occupied, London burning, and the Wehrmacht apparently unstoppable, an American philosophy professor published a book explaining that none of it meant what people thought it meant. The war, he argued, was not a struggle between freedom and tyranny, or capitalism and socialism. It was a civil war inside a single worldwide revolution that had already happened, and that almost no one had noticed, because it had happened without barricades: the revolution by which the men who manage – the executives, the production engineers, the bureau chiefs, the planners – were replacing the men who own as the ruling class of the earth. Nazi Germany was one version of the new order. Stalin's Russia was a second. And Roosevelt's New Deal America, the professor added, to the lasting fury of his American readers, was an earlier and politer stage of the same thing. The author was James Burnham, and the biography matters as much as with Whyte, though it points the other way. Whyte was an insider describing the middle from inside. Burnham was a serial apostate describing the top from a great height. A professor at New York University, he had spent the thirties as perhaps the leading intellectual of American Trotskyism, co-running its journal, corresponding with Trotsky himself in exile. In nineteen forty he broke – not just with Trotsky but with Marxism entire – over a question that sounds scholastic and is not: what was the Soviet Union? Orthodoxy said a workers' state, deformed but salvageable. Burnham looked at it and reported what he saw: a new kind of class rule, neither capitalist nor socialist, in which the men who controlled the state's productive machinery had become masters of everything, with the workers as dispossessed as ever. Having seen it in Russia, he then did what converts of his intensity do, and saw it everywhere. The Managerial Revolution was written in roughly a year of ferocious certainty, sold enormously, terrified and thrilled its readers, and set the terms of an argument about managers and power that ran through the decade's most serious minds. The Annotated Shelf has spent six episodes among the descendants of that argument. This episode reads the ancestor – and then reads the man who took it apart.

Chapter Two: The Argument, Steelmanned

The book deserves its strongest form first, and its strongest form starts from an observation that was not Burnham's and was not controversial. In nineteen thirty-two, two Columbia scholars, Adolf Berle and Gardiner Means, had documented something structural about the modern corporation: ownership had separated from control. The great firms were owned by thousands of scattered shareholders who controlled nothing, and controlled by salaried executives who owned almost nothing. The capitalist of the textbooks – the man who owned the mill and ran the mill – was already a fossil in the American economy's leading firms, and Berle and Means put a magnitude on the fossil's replacement: the two hundred largest corporations, run almost entirely by men who did not own them, controlled something like half the corporate wealth of the United States. Burnham took that finding and asked the Marxist's question with the Marxism removed: if ownership and control have come apart, which one is the ruling class made of? His answer: control, always control. Legal title is paper; the class that actually operates the instruments of production – that decides what is made, where, by whom – will sooner or later take the surplus, the status, and the state. The managers did not need to want this, and that is the argument's coldest and best feature. It is not a conspiracy theory. Burnham's managers are not plotting in a cellar; they are simply the only people who can run the machinery of an industrial civilization that has become too complex for owners to operate or workers to seize, and power flows to them the way water flows downhill, war by war, agency by agency, merger by merger. Every crisis ratchets it: complexity demands coordination, coordination demands managers, and no crisis ever demands fewer of them. Burnham did not have to wait long for a demonstration, because the largest one in American history began seven months after his book appeared. Mobilization for the war handed the economy to exactly the class he had named. Production schedules, materials priorities, price ceilings, the allocation of steel and rubber and manpower – decisions the market had made in nineteen twenty-nine were made in nineteen forty-three by boards, and the boards were staffed by executives on loan from the corporations and administrators on loan from the agencies, planning production for a nation as a single enterprise. The owners still owned everything, and decided almost nothing. When the war ended, the price controls lapsed and the boards dissolved, but the demonstration did not un-happen: American industry had been run for four years as a managed system, it had out-produced the planet, and the men who had managed it went back to their firms and their bureaus knowing what they now knew. The reader of nineteen forty-six, looking back at the book of nineteen forty-one, could be forgiven for thinking the professor had called it. On this reading, fascism, Stalinism, and the New Deal really were variants of one process – not morally equivalent, but structurally kin: in each, the crisis of the thirties transferred command of the economy from owners and markets to administrators and plans. And before you dismiss the extension to America as thirties fever, run the argument forward past Burnham's horizon and watch what it picks up. The postwar economy Whyte photographed – the benevolent corporation, the executive suite unmoored from any owner's eye, the state grown into the economy's largest planner – is recognizably Burnham's world at cruising altitude. Galbraith would describe its technostructure in the sixties; the shareholder-value counterrevolution of the eighties, which this series met in the Davies episodes as Friedman's objective function, only makes sense as a counter-revolution – capital's armed expedition to retake territory the managers had held for two generations. You do not get to call the revolution imaginary and then spend nineteen eighty onward reversing it.

Chapter Three: Orwell's Innings

And yet the book is remembered, when it is remembered, mostly as the target of one of the great demolitions in the English essay, and the demolition is deserved. George Orwell read Burnham the way this series tries to read everything – twice, once for the structure and once for the tells – and in nineteen forty-six, in a small journal called Polemic, he published Second Thoughts on James Burnham. The essay's method is the thing to learn from. Orwell does not argue with Burnham's theory first. He simply lists what Burnham had predicted, next to what happened. In nineteen forty, with Germany ascendant, Burnham had treated German victory as effectively settled and described the coming world accordingly. By nineteen forty-four, with the Red Army advancing, his new book found the future belonging to a Soviet-dominated order, and the analysis adjusted itself around the new inevitability with barely a stumble. Orwell's sentence for this habit is fourteen words long and it is the essay in miniature: at each point Burnham is predicting a continuation of the thing that is happening. And then Orwell goes one layer down, past the method to the motive, and names the disease: power worship. Burnham's forecasting kept failing in the same direction because some part of him was enchanted by the winners – power at its most brutal struck him as power at its most real, and so whoever was currently winning appeared to him as the future itself. The cruelty of the diagnosis is that it converts Burnham's tone, all that granite realism, into evidence against him: the man advertising his freedom from wishful thinking was doing wishful thinking of a rarer kind, wishing on behalf of whoever held the whip. Sit this beside the shelf's own instruments and it clicks into a familiar socket. The realist's temptation is the identity dose – the reader of Jackall or Davies or Burnham who graduates from these systems contain brutal dynamics to only the brutal dynamics are real, at which point he has stopped analyzing power and started rooting for it. Orwell caught the overdose in its most distinguished patient, and the prescription label this series keeps re-printing – diagnostic doses medicine, identity doses poison – is, in three words, what that essay taught. One more turn, though, because the relationship did not end in refutation. Orwell kept what he had killed. The world of Nineteen Eighty-Four – three managerial super-states, permanently at war, each unconquerable, each ruled by an oligarchy that worships power for its own sake – is Burnham's geography with Burnham's psychology installed as the state religion. Orwell thought the prediction was false as forecast and true as temptation, so he wrote it as a warning instead. The most influential political novel of the century is a refuted book, running in emulation. As for Burnham himself, the rest of the life confirms the diagnosis without softening it. He kept the method – find the great struggle, pick the side history has already chosen, announce the choice as realism – and rode it rightward for four decades: an early book on Machiavelli and his heirs that treated all politics as elite rotation and is, quietly, his best; consulting work for the early Cold War intelligence apparatus; then a founding seat at National Review, where his column advocated waging the Cold War as precisely the kind of ruthless great-power contest his books had described. Ronald Reagan hung the Presidential Medal of Freedom on him in nineteen eighty-three, citing his influence on how America saw the world, which was true, and which is its own kind of unsettling: the man Orwell diagnosed with power worship ended his career decorated by power, for services to its self-understanding.

Chapter Four: The Twins, Face to Face

Put the two books on the table together now, because each one holds the page the other is missing. Whyte's question was, what does the organization believe? Burnham's was, who rules? Whyte answered his own question with fieldwork and could not answer Burnham's; his book finds a middle class converted to the Social Ethic and never asks in whose interest the conversion runs. Burnham answered his own question with a theory and could not answer Whyte's; his managers are chess pieces with job titles, and nothing in The Managerial Revolution can explain why a Park Forest wife schedules coffee or why a junior executive lies moderately on a personality test. Read together, they interlock into one machine seen from two floors. Burnham names the structure: an industrial world that had made its administrators indispensable and was reorganizing command around them. Whyte names the software: the belief system that made membership in that structure feel like morality, so that the new order could be staffed by volunteers who experienced their absorption as belonging. The revolution needed no secret police in America because it had belongingness instead. And the shelf's later books slot into the gap between the twins with an exactness that is the real payoff of reading the ancestors. Rao's Gervais Principle, the series' founding text, is Whyte with the reverence removed: his Clueless layer – the loyal, over-performing middle that identifies with the firm – is the organization man three generations on, still converted, now named without pity; Rao knew it, and began a chapter-by-chapter reading of Whyte on his blog in two thousand and eight, a planned eight-part series that stalled three posts in, the year before The Office swallowed his attention and produced the essays this feed descends from. Jackall's Moral Mazes is the dark sequel neither twin foresaw: the organization man's grandchildren, the belief burned off, the belonging now purely tactical – the Social Ethic decayed from a faith into a survival kit. And Davies closes the loop with the correction Burnham needed most. The Unaccountability Machine episodes established that the modern organization computes its decisions through structures no individual controls, and that question, asked at the Post Office or the insurer – who decided? – kept returning the answer: the machine decided. Now run that answer back against nineteen forty-one. Burnham saw command migrating out of the owners' hands and assumed it must be migrating into someone else's – a class inherits, because in every previous revolution a class inherited. The shelf's colder finding is that he tracked the migration correctly and misread the destination. Command left the owners and did not arrive at the managers. It dissolved into the procedures between them. The managers did not become the masters of the machine; they became its components – better paid than the workers, more comfortable, and, as any of Jackall's vice presidents could testify, no more in command of the objective function than the postmasters were. Part two of the Davies series said it in this decade's vocabulary: the corporation is an artificial intelligence that runs on people the way software runs on silicon, and nobody claims that the silicon is in charge. The revolution happened. The throne it built is empty. And Rao's coldest chapter, read back through Burnham, names the ones who noticed. The Sociopath layer of the Gervais Principle is not Burnham's ruling class, because it does not rule the machine either; what it does is what episode five of this feed found at the top of every sink – it positions itself where the unattenuated information flows, treats the empty throne as a vacancy to arbitrage rather than a seat to occupy, and moves on before the procedures close over it. Burnham predicted masters. The machine age produced, at its most knowing, squatters. That is not a comfort; an empty throne cannot be negotiated with, voted out, or shamed. It is, however, a different problem from the one Burnham announced, and mistaking the second for the first – hunting a ruling class where there is an unaccountable process – is a way of being angry at the wrong address for an entire lifetime.

Chapter Five: Verdict, Dose, and the Question for Monday

The verdict, then, on the pair. The Organization Man is the better book by every measure a reader can use: grounded where Burnham is oracular, humane where Burnham is chilly, and still accurate about the texture of institutional life – the meetings, the tests, the moralized fitting-in – in a way that survives every change of costume. Its famous obsolescence keeps failing to arrive. Nocera's two thousand and two foreword assumed the layoffs of the eighties had killed the organization man; two decades later the loyal corporation is indeed dead, and yet the Social Ethic is doing fine, running on new hardware – the culture-fit interview is a personality test with the scoring key hidden, the open-plan office is a Park Forest court with worse acoustics, and a workforce told to be passionate about the mission is being asked for exactly the interior surrender Whyte said no employer had a right to request, minus the pension that was the old regime's side of the bargain. Read it whole, once, and the appendix twice. The Managerial Revolution earns a different prescription: read it the way Orwell read it, with the essay alongside as the antidote – the book for the structure it names, the essay for the failure mode it demonstrates, because Burnham teaches how organizational power actually pools, and Orwell teaches what believing only that does to a mind. The dose warning on this pairing is the strongest the series has issued, since each book is the other's overdose: enough Whyte with no Burnham and you become the adjusted man who thinks the group is always right; enough Burnham with no Whyte and you become the realist rooting for the whip. And the question to carry into Monday is the one the twins ask together, pointed at your own week. Find the nearest place where your organization asked for fit rather than work – a test, an interview stage, a value stated as a personality trait – and ask Burnham's question about it: who, or what, does this selection actually serve? If you can name a person, you have found a manager worth arguing with. If you cannot – if the fitting serves nothing but the process that measures it – then you are standing where the twins' two diagnoses meet, looking at a machine selecting for the people least likely to ask what it is for. And one account from these two episodes remains open. Twice now this series has caught the organization man's world resting on work it never put on the books – the coffee circuits of Park Forest, the vetted marriage – and twice the observation went by in a subordinate clause, which is exactly the treatment Whyte gave it. Before the queue moves on, that ledger gets read in full. Next time, a third part on The Organization Man: the wife, the curriculum, and the exit. Thanks for listening.

Chapter One: The Appendix That Teaches You to Lie

Somewhere in America, in the spring of nineteen fifty-five, a young man in a good suit sat down in a personnel office and picked up a pencil. In front of him was a booklet of several hundred statements, and his job was to agree or disagree with each one. I feel that people are watching me. I prefer a quiet evening at home to a party. My mother was a good woman. His answers would be scored against a profile, and the profile would decide whether he was suited to a career at the company – not whether he could do the work, but whether he was the kind of person who fit. He had probably taken a test like this to get into college, and another to get his commission in the service, and he would take more of them, at promotions and transfers, for the rest of his working life. He answered carefully, and what he was careful about is the whole subject of this episode: he tried to guess what a normal man would say, and to say that. A year later he could have bought help. In the back of one of the best-selling books of nineteen fifty-six, past the final chapter, sits an appendix with a title that would be a joke if the author were joking: How to Cheat on Personality Tests. It is a practical manual. It tells the reader that the tests cannot really be beaten by honesty, walks him through the logic of the scoring, and advises him, whenever in doubt, to give the most conventional answer he can construct – to report that he loves his wife and his work in that order, moderately, and that he rarely feels strongly about anything. The book containing this appendix was not a piece of underground samizdat. It was written by an editor of Fortune, the most establishment business magazine in the country, published by Simon and Schuster, and bought by two million people, a large fraction of whom were exactly the young men the tests were built to sort. The author was William Hollingsworth Whyte, and the fact that his book about corporate America ends with instructions for deceiving corporate America is not a stunt bolted onto a work of sociology. It is the argument, compressed. To see why a Fortune editor came to believe that lying to the personnel department was an ethical act – close to a duty – you have to follow him through the book, and the book is where this series has been heading for six episodes, because nearly everything the Annotated Shelf has read so far descends from it.

Chapter Two: The Insider

Start with who he was, because the book's authority hangs on it. Whyte was nobody's outsider. Princeton, class of nineteen thirty-nine; the Marine Corps through Guadalcanal; then Fortune, where he rose through the ranks writing about business for businessmen. He was not a professor with a theory, and his politics were, if anything, conservative in the older sense – he admired enterprise and he liked executives. In March of nineteen fifty-two he published an article in Fortune about the growing pressure toward unanimous thinking in American life, and needed a word for it, so he built one on the chassis Orwell had used in Nineteen Eighty-Four, three years earlier, for doublethink. Whyte's coinage was groupthink. The word escaped the article, wandered through the culture, got formalized by an academic psychologist two decades later, and now lives in every management-training deck in the world, usually without a trace of the man who made it. That small theft set the pattern of Whyte's whole career: he saw things about organizations a decade before the people paid to see them, described what he saw in plain declarative prose, and then watched the vocabulary get taken while the argument was left behind. And the position he described it all from matters as much as the seeing. C. Wright Mills, the Columbia sociologist whose radical study of the American elite came out the same year, reviewed Whyte's book for the New York Times and could barely conceal his irritation: an energetic reporter, Mills allowed, working a very old theme, keeping the tone of an earnest, optimistic Boy Scout. Mills wanted a prosecution and got a field guide. But the field guide has outlived the prosecution, and I think the reason is precisely the thing Mills sneered at. Whyte liked the people he was studying. He was one of them. When such a man tells you, in the calmest voice imaginable, that something has gone wrong with the moral core of American work, the calm is the evidence.

Chapter Three: The Belief

So what had gone wrong? Here is where the book surprises anyone who knows it only by reputation, because the reputation says it is a book about conformity, and Whyte goes out of his way, in the first pages, to say it is not – or rather, that conformity is the symptom and he is after the disease. His opening sentence is seven words long: this book is about the organization man. And his central claim is that the organization man is not a coward. He is a convert. Something had happened, Whyte argued, to the operating faith of the American middle class. The old faith – call it the Protestant Ethic, as Whyte did, borrowing from Weber – held that salvation came through individual effort: thrift, competition, the lonely struggle upward, the self as the unit that God and the market kept accounts on. That ethic was officially still in force; every commencement speaker and company chairman recited it. But the lived faith, the one that actually governed conduct, had quietly become something else, and Whyte gave it a name built for contrast: the Social Ethic. He defined it with an engineer's precision as the body of thought that makes morally legitimate the pressures of society against the individual, and he broke it into three load-bearing propositions. That the group, not the individual, is the true source of creativity. That belongingness is the deepest need of the individual – his word, belongingness, and the quotation marks around it in the book carry a full chapter of contempt. And that science – testing, measurement, adjustment – can deliver that belonging, engineer it, guarantee it. Sit with the structure of that for a moment, because it explains everything the book then documents. If the group is where ideas come from, then the lone dissenter is not brave, he is malfunctioning. If belonging is the ultimate need, then making someone fit is not oppression, it is therapy. And if science can measure fit, then the personality test is not an intrusion, it is a diagnosis kindly offered. The Social Ethic does not force anyone to conform. It redescribes conformity as health, and resistance as a symptom. That move – the redescription, not the pressure – is what Whyte spent four hundred pages hunting, and it is why he insisted the organization man was worse off than a man merely oppressed. A man oppressed knows which direction freedom is. A man converted has agreed to forget.

Chapter Four: The Laboratory on the Prairie

A belief system, though, is hard to photograph, and the lasting greatness of the book is that Whyte went and photographed it anyway. Thirty miles south of Chicago, on former farmland, a developer had built a town called Park Forest: thousands of rental garden apartments and small houses, arranged in courts, filling up as fast as they could be finished with junior executives, engineers, and salesmen in their late twenties – organization men in their larval stage, plus their wives and small children. Whyte treated it the way an anthropologist treats an island, and Fortune let him: he interviewed, mapped, counted, and moved through the courts for months, across several years of visits. What he found is the part of the book that reads best today, because it is pure observation and the observation is uncanny. These were the most transient people in America – the average family would be transferred within three years, and they knew it – and instead of the rootlessness making them solitary, it made them ferociously social. Not knowing anyone, and knowing they would soon leave whomever they met, they built instant community the way the Army builds camps: joinable on arrival, standardized, and portable. Dozens of clubs and committees per court. A church deliberately designed without denominational edges, so that no newcomer could fail to qualify. Coffee circulating between kitchens all day on a schedule everyone denied existed and everyone knew. And then the observation that made the book's method famous. Whyte mapped which families were friends with which, and found that the single best predictor was not class, not religion, not temperament, but architecture. Friendship followed the placement of driveways, stoops, and courts; social life ran along the lines the site planner had drawn, and a family placed at an awkward corner could be effectively alone for years through no fault of anyone's. He put maps in the book. You can look at the diagram of a court and read off, from the geometry, who had coffee with whom. The residents half knew it, and it unsettled them when they saw it stated. The economics of the courts ran on the same current, and in a direction the satirists of suburbia never got right. The reflex Whyte found was not keeping up with the Joneses; it was keeping down with them. Display was the sin. A man who came into money did not parade it; he apologized for it, spent it quietly or not at all, because a purchase that rose above the court's waterline was a claim to be different, and difference was the one luxury the group taxed. Whyte watched families calibrate their furniture, their cars, and their opinions to the middle of the block with the precision of pilots holding formation, and he understood what he was watching: not envy, which is at least an individualist's vice, but the Social Ethic doing its housekeeping – the group grinding off whatever protruded, gently, socially, over coffee. It should unsettle you in a different way: this is the third proposition of the Social Ethic – science achieving belongingness – functioning perfectly. The developers read Whyte's findings with interest, and began designing the courts to produce community on purpose. The suburb was not a picture of the organization; it was the organization's training environment, and what it trained was the reflex of adjusting. When the group's norms pinched, the Park Forester did not ask whether the norms were right. He asked what was wrong with his fit.

Chapter Five: The Machinery of Fit

Which returns us to the young man with the pencil, because the personality test is where the Social Ethic stopped being an atmosphere and became an instrument. By the mid-fifties, testing was an industry. A majority of large American corporations screened applicants or candidates for promotion with instruments claiming to measure adjustment, stability, sociability – the traits of the man who would fit – and the tests' assumptions were the Social Ethic written into scoring keys: the well-adjusted man agrees with most people; strong feeling is a warning sign; the ideal profile sits reassuringly near the middle of every scale. The items themselves deserve a moment of dwelling, because their texture is the argument. Do you daydream frequently. Do you sometimes feel self-conscious. Would you rather read a book than go bowling with the office. There is no competent answer to such questions, only a normal one, and the applicant knew it, which is why the instrument measured, in practice, exactly one trait: the ability to guess what the company wanted a soul to look like, and to produce that soul on paper under time pressure. An examination that can only be passed by impersonation had, without anyone deciding it, made impersonation the entry-level skill of managerial life. Whyte's assault on this machinery runs on two rails, and the first is the one a clinician will recognize as home ground: the tests did not work even on their own terms. Their validation was circular – the profile of a good executive was built by testing incumbent executives, so the instrument could only ever certify resemblance to the men already in the chair. The scores predicted little; the norms enforced much. This series has a name for that shape. A measure had become a target, and what the target actually optimized was not performance but similarity – Goodhart's law, operating thirty years before Goodhart stated it, with human personalities as the gamed metric. But it is Whyte's second rail that cuts deeper, and he is explicit that it matters more. Suppose the tests worked, he says. Suppose the science were sound. It would still be wrong – because the question the test asks, who are you, underneath, when your guard is down, is a question no employer has a right to ask. The work is owed; the self is not. A company entitled to your soul on the day of hiring is a company that has abolished the line between employment and membership, and membership of the total kind was exactly what the benevolent corporation of nineteen fifty-six was learning to want – not the grasping company town of the robber barons, but something softer and therefore harder to fight: the organization that loves you, tests you because it loves you, and adjusts you for your own good. Now the appendix stops being a joke and becomes the book's ethics distilled. You cannot refuse the test; refusal is a profile too. You cannot answer honestly; honesty hands over what is not owed. So you lie – blandly, moderately, in the direction of the group – and Whyte, the Princeton Marine, the Fortune editor, the man Mills called a Boy Scout, walks you through it step by step. It is civil disobedience for the gray-flannel set: the one place in the book where the diagnosis turns into an instruction, and the instruction is, defend the border. Give the organization its work and its loyalty. Keep the self.

Chapter Six: What the Boy Scout Could Not See

The case against the book has had seventy years to assemble, and its strongest counts should be stated the way its friends would not. Mills's count came first and still stands: as social theory, the book is thin. Whyte names a belief system but never explains where it came from or what interests it serves; the Social Ethic simply arrives, like weather. Ask who benefits when a generation of middle-class men equates dissent with maladjustment, and the book goes quiet – it describes the species exquisitely and never asks who runs the zoo. The second count is the one the book cannot see because its author was standing inside it: the organization man's whole world rested on an unexamined support called the organization man's wife. Whyte interviewed the wives at length – some of the book's best pages are about the company's growing interest in vetting them – and the coffee circuits of Park Forest that he mapped were, in every particular, women's labor. The book registers all of it as scenery. That the Social Ethic pressed on the woman with no office to escape to, all day, with no appendix teaching her to cheat, is a sentence Whyte never quite writes. And the third count is about the prescription. Defend the border, keep the self – it is advice for one man at a time, and it concedes the terrain in the act of defending it, because a border defended in secret, by strategic blandness on a form, leaves the machinery entirely intact for the next applicant. Joseph Nocera, introducing the book's re-issue in two thousand and two, took it for granted that history had simply dissolved the problem – the layoffs of the eighties killed the loyal corporation, the entrepreneur returned, the organization man died of obsolescence. For a while that read as the verdict. I do not think it survives contact with the present, but the case for that belongs at the end of the series, when the verdict comes. What belongs here is the question the book leaves smoking on the table. Whyte proved that the middle of the American organization had converted to a new faith, and traced the faith into the suburbs, the churches, the marriage, the scoring keys – everywhere except upward. Fifteen years before Park Forest poured its first foundation, another American had looked at the same managerial world from the opposite end and answered the question Whyte never asked. Not, what does the organization believe? But: who rules? His answer was that the managers – not the owners, not the workers, not the elected – were becoming the ruling class of the entire industrial world, in Washington and Moscow and Berlin alike, and that the process was as unstoppable as it was invisible to the people it was happening to. He was a philosophy professor, an ex-Trotskyist, and the most spectacularly wrong right man of his century, and George Orwell built Nineteen Eighty-Four partly out of arguing with him. Next time, the political twin of The Organization Man: James Burnham's The Managerial Revolution. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Unaccountability Machine, Part Three: Repairing the Feedback
item.description: The final part on Dan Davies's book: what repair would actually take, the critics given their full say, the synthesis with Rao and Jackall extended, and a verdict with a dose.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Industry That Chose the Other Road
